I get in part what he's saying, that there are too many people who call them selves christians without walking the walk, but that doesn't mean we're supposed to make christianity some exclusive club with ranks and eligibility requirements. In fact, in my understanding, that's directly contradictory to what Christ would want. Everyone falls short of God's glory, thats going to happen no matter what. Furthermore, some people will fall short more openly than others. King David fell short of God's grace when he got another man's wife pregnant and then had her husband killed in battle. That's pretty disgraceful, but we still remember David as a great, God honoring, king - and rightfully so.

The minute we start excluding people from christianity is the minute we go against all that it stands for. Everyone is a child of God, and everyone is given the chance to be saved. The author says just believing in Jesus isn't enough, which I can agree with. But I still believe that being saved is as simple as believing in Jesus - the son of the one true God, believing that he died for your sins, then repenting of those sins. Simple as that, because salvation is truly a gift. People ask how the ten commandments fit in to that. In my opinion, the ten commandments are how you show your appreciation of the gift of salvation and grow closer to God. Anyone who gets saved then disregards the ten commandments is forgetting the important last step, repent. I think here is where the author is saying that these people should not be called christians. And again, I see where he is coming from, since their faith is certainly in danger, but I still believe it is not our place to judge. We should never be going around telling people "you're not a christian", because then we are no longer being a loving body of Christ, but an accusing body talking down to people who need help.

TL;DR: In my opinion, no person should be telling another person "you're not a christian". Everyone falls short of God, including those of us attempting to judge those very same people.

I think that that is as simple making a distinction between saying "you're not a christian" and "what you're saying goes against biblical doctrine". I'm not a Catholic. But here's my reasoning why Catholicism is "American Christianity":

According to PEW research, 70.6% identify as Christian in the US, with only 20.8% identifying as Catholic vs. 51.3% identifying as protestant (that's on page 4). Yet, when you burrow into the report (page 21), you'll see the largest section of Protestants are Baptists (25.4%), and of the Baptists, the Southern Baptist convention is the largest at 5.3%

I have attended both Southern Baptist and Freewill Baptist services, and these congregations and their beliefs are different. You can call them both Baptists, but that like grouping Catholics with Protestants because they all call themselves Christians. You're grouping by name (or label, if you will), not by belief.

If you want to actually look at participants of a specific belief of Christianity, that's 20.8% Catholics vs. 5.3% Southern Baptists. From this point of view, Catholics are the largest branch of people who call themselves Christian who share the same beliefs in the USA.
